subject: math

unit.title: Fractions of shapes and quantities
unit.essentialQuestion: What does each part of a fraction tell us, and how do we find a fraction of a number?

title: Fractions of a quantity
objectives: By the end, I can find a unit and non-unit fraction of an amount by sharing.

vocabulary.definition: a fair share of a group of things, not just of one shape
deal one-to-each into equal piles until everything is gone
a fraction with 1 on top — just one of the equal parts
a fraction with more than 1 on top — several of the equal parts
the bottom number — it tells you how many equal piles to share into
vocabulary.example: the 4 in ¼ means share into 4 plates

emphasize: The bottom number tells you HOW MANY PLATES: ¼ of an amount means share into 4 equal piles, then count ONE pile.
¾ means count THREE of the four piles — top number = how many piles you take.
Pre-empt the trap: ¼ of 12 is NOT 12 − 4. We SHARE, we don't take away.

keyConcepts: fraction of an amount by equal sharing
denominator = number of piles, numerator = piles you count
¼ of 12 = 12 ÷ 4 — fractions ride on division
misconceptions: stopping at one pile for a non-unit fraction: '¾ of 12 = 3'
sharing into the wrong number of piles (using the top number, or a guess)
dealing unequally so the piles don't match
hooks: I've got 12 sweets and I want to give you a QUARTER of them — how many is that?
priorKnowledge: a quarter = one of 4 equal parts (Lesson 13)

digital: steps card for the share-then-count routine

video.searchTerm: find a quarter of an amount KS1
video.watchTask: Every time an amount gets shared, say how many plates BEFORE the video shows them — the bottom number gives it away.

afterCheck.question: To find a quarter of an amount, how many equal groups do you share into?

plan.goal: Pose the ¼-of-12 puzzle; retrieve one-to-each dealing from Lesson 11.
plan.note: Leave the puzzle open — the child suggests a method. The sweets sliding forward invitingly is the moment.
plan.successCriteria: Child recalls 'deal one to each pile until gone' from the division lessons.

script.say: I've got 12 sweets here… and I want to give you a QUARTER of them. Ooh — how many sweets is that? Hmm. How could we work it out fairly? … Think back: when we shared 12 between 3 last week, what did we do?
script.adaptHints: Swap sweets for the child's favourite treat. Listen for 'dealt one to each pile until gone' — that memory is the whole method.

blocks.caption: 12 sweets… and you get a QUARTER of them. How many?

stuckProtocol: If dealing is forgotten: quick replay — 'like dealing cards: one, one, one… round and round until they're gone.'

plan.goal: Model the method: ¼ means 4 plates; deal all 12 one-to-each; count ONE plate → 3; link to 12 ÷ 4.
plan.note: Anchor phrase: 'the bottom number tells me how many plates.' Show the division link explicitly — fractions ride on the division they already own.
plan.successCriteria: Child sees the full deal into 4 plates, one plate highlighted, and hears '¼ of 12 = 3 — the same as 12 ÷ 4'.

script.say: A quarter means FOUR equal parts — so the bottom number, 4, tells me how many plates I need. Watch me deal all 12, one to each plate, round and round: one, two, three, four… one, two, three, four… one, two, three, four — all gone! Every plate has 3. Now, a quarter is just ONE of those plates — so ¼ of 12 is 3. And do you see the old friend hiding here? Sharing 12 into 4 plates is exactly 12 ÷ 4. Fractions of amounts are division wearing a party hat!
script.adaptHints: Deal with the same card-dealing rhythm as Lesson 11 so the method feels familiar. Land hard on 'the bottom number tells me how many plates.'

blocks.title: Fraction of an amount — the routine
steps: Read the BOTTOM number — that's how many plates
Deal one-to-each until everything is gone
Count the plates the TOP number asks for

plan.goal: The child finds ¾ of 12: same 4 plates, but now count THREE of them → 9.
plan.note: The plates are already dealt from the explain — the only new move is counting three plates instead of one. Scribe '¾ of 12 = 9' when the child lands it.
plan.successCriteria: Child says 4 plates, counts three plates (3 + 3 + 3) and completes ¾ of 12 = 9.

script.say: Your turn to be the dealer — let's find ¾ of 12. First question: the bottom number is still 4, so… how many plates? … Four! Deal them out — 3 on each, just like before. Now the top number is 3 — so how many plates do we count this time? … Three plates: 3, 6, 9! One plate was ¼ = 3, so three plates, ¾, is…?
script.adaptHints: If the child says '3' (one plate), point at the top number: 'the 3 on top says count THREE plates.' Celebrate 3 + 3 + 3 or 3 × 3 language.

blocks.text: ¾ of 12 = ___ (share into 4 plates of 3, count 3 plates)

check.question: One plate is ¼ = 3. So three plates, ¾ of 12, is…?

wrongAnswers.why: stopped at one plate — gave the quarter
wrongAnswers.remedy: That's ¼ — one plate. The top number says count THREE plates: 3, 6…

wrongAnswers.why: did 12 − 4 — subtracted the denominator
wrongAnswers.remedy: We SHARE, we don't take away. The plates are right there — count three of them.

plan.goal: The key diagnostic: ¾ of 12 — catches both the 12 − 4 subtracters and the one-plate stoppers.
plan.note: Fresh ask, no plates pre-dealt this time. Always probe 'how did the plates help?' after a correct answer.
plan.successCriteria: Child answers 9 and explains via the plates (4 plates of 3, count 3 plates).

script.say: Checkpoint, dealer! No plates on screen this time — picture them in your head. What is ¾ of 12? … And tell me: how did the plates help you get it?
script.adaptHints: If the child hesitates, offer the routine, not the answer: 'bottom number first — how many plates?'

options: 9 — share into 4 plates of 3, count 3 plates
blocks.explain: Share 12 into 4 equal plates (3 each), then count three plates: 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.

wrongAnswers.why: subtracted the denominator (12 − 4) instead of sharing
wrongAnswers.remedy: We SHARE, not take away. Deal 12 into 4 plates — now count what's in three of them.

wrongAnswers.why: stopped at one plate — gave ¼ instead of ¾
wrongAnswers.remedy: ¾ means THREE of the four plates — count three: 3, 6…

plan.goal: Independent fractions of amounts: ¼ of 8, ½ of 10, ¾ of 8, recorded as 'share into __ plates, count __'.
plan.note: Director draws from the practiceBank, start level 2. Have the child SAY the routine ('share into 4, count 1') before each answer — the sentence is the scaffold. New denominator (⅓ → 3 plates) only once secure.
plan.successCriteria: Child solves 3+ items including one unit and one non-unit fraction, stating the plate count each time.

script.say: Practice time at the fair-share café! Orders are coming in — a quarter of this, three-quarters of that. For every order, tell me the recipe first: share into how many plates, count how many? Then serve the answer. First customer's here!
script.adaptHints: Frame amounts with the child's interests (grapes, football cards, gems). Never change the numbers.

stuckProtocol: Name why: 'the 4 got taken away instead of shared' or 'we counted one plate too few.'
Go fully concrete: deal the counters onto plates together on screen, one at a time.
One hint: 'Bottom number = number of plates.'
Re-ask with ½ of 6, then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'

plan.goal: Child states the steps for ¾ of a number; end on an earned win.
plan.note: Child-led; the character listens. The two-step recipe in their own words is the evidence.
plan.successCriteria: Child says 'share into 4 equal piles, then count 3 of them' (own words fine).

script.say: Last order of the day: tell me YOUR recipe for finding ¾ of a number. … Perfect — share into four equal piles, count three! You dealt one-to-each instead of guessing, every single time — fair sharing is the secret to fractions, and you've cracked it.
script.adaptHints: Praise the observed process: saying the recipe before solving, dealing fairly, catching the 12 − 4 trap.

block.explain: Share 6 into 2 equal plates — 3 on each. One plate is ½: 3 grapes.

wrongAnswers.why: did 6 − 2 — subtracted the denominator
wrongAnswers.remedy: We share, we don't take away. Deal 6 onto 2 plates — how many on one plate?

wrongAnswers.why: kept the whole amount — didn't share
wrongAnswers.remedy: Half means the grapes get SPLIT between 2 plates. Deal them and count one plate.

hints: The 2 on the bottom means 2 plates.
Deal one-to-each: how many on each plate?

reteach.say: Half of 6: two plates, deal them out — one, one… two, two… three, three. Three on each plate. ½ of 6 = 3, the same as 6 ÷ 2.

block.text: ¼ of 4 cookies: share into 4 plates — each plate gets ___ cookie(s).

wrongAnswers.why: kept the whole amount instead of sharing
wrongAnswers.remedy: Four cookies, four plates — deal one-to-each. How many lands on each plate?

wrongAnswers.why: thinks 4 shared into 4 leaves nothing
wrongAnswers.remedy: The cookies don't vanish — they spread out! Deal them: one plate, one cookie.

hints: One round of dealing and they're gone.

reteach.say: Four cookies, four plates: one, one, one, one — done in a single round! Each plate holds exactly 1. ¼ of 4 = 1.

wrongAnswers.why: did 8 − 4 — subtracted the denominator
wrongAnswers.remedy: The 4 tells you how many PLATES, not what to take away. Deal 8 into 4 plates.

wrongAnswers.why: didn't share at all
wrongAnswers.remedy: A quarter is a SHARE of the 8, so it must be smaller. Deal into 4 plates and count one.

reteach.say: ¼ of 8: four plates, deal all 8 — one round puts 1 on each, second round makes it 2 on each, all gone. One plate is 2. ¼ of 8 = 8 ÷ 4 = 2.

wrongAnswers.why: did 12 − 4 — the classic subtract-the-denominator trap
wrongAnswers.remedy: We SHARE, we don't take away! Deal 12 into 4 plates — count one plate.

wrongAnswers.why: counted three plates — gave ¾ instead of ¼
wrongAnswers.remedy: The top number is 1 — count just ONE plate.

reteach.say: Watch the trap: 12 − 4 = 8 is TAKE-AWAY maths, and fractions are SHARING maths. Deal 12 into 4 plates: 3 each. ¼ of 12 = 3 — division in a party hat!

wrongAnswers.why: stopped at one plate — gave ¼
wrongAnswers.remedy: The 3 on top says count THREE plates: 2, 4…

wrongAnswers.why: did 8 − 3 — subtracted the numerator
wrongAnswers.remedy: No taking away! Share 8 into 4 plates of 2, then count three plates.

hints: Share into 4 plates first — 2 on each.

reteach.say: ¾ of 8, the two-step dance: share 8 into 4 plates — 2 each. Then count three plates: 2, 4, 6. ¾ of 8 = 6. Quarter first, then three of them!

block.caption: ¾ of 8 — count 3 of the 4 plates = 6

block.prompt: To find ⅓ of 9, how many plates do you share into?
block.explain: The bottom number of ⅓ is 3 — share into 3 equal plates, then count one.

wrongAnswers.why: used the amount instead of the denominator
wrongAnswers.remedy: The 9 is what you're sharing OUT. The bottom number of the fraction tells you the plates.

wrongAnswers.why: used the numerator for the plates
wrongAnswers.remedy: The top number is how many plates you COUNT at the end. The bottom number sets the plates.

hints: Look at the BOTTOM number of ⅓.
Bottom = plates; top = plates you count.

reteach.say: The fraction is a recipe card: bottom number = how many plates on the table; top number = how many plates you count at the end. ⅓ → three plates, count one. Read the recipe before you cook!

block.caption: Bottom sets the plates, top says how many to count

block.prompt: Match each order to its answer (share 8 into 4 plates of 2 first!).

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: ½ of 8→4, ¼ of 8→2, ¾ of 8→6, ¼ of 20→5

wrongAnswers.why: counted one plate for a non-unit fraction
wrongAnswers.remedy: ¾ counts THREE plates of 2 — skip them: 2, 4, 6.

wrongAnswers.why: did 20 − 4
wrongAnswers.remedy: Share, don't subtract: 20 into 4 plates — how many on one plate?

hints: Do ¼ of 8 first — the others build on it.
¾ is three times the ¼ answer.

reteach.say: Fractions of 8 are a family: ¼ of 8 is 2 — one plate. ½ is two plates: 4. ¾ is three plates: 6. Find the quarter first and the rest is counting plates!

block.prompt: New denominator! What is ⅓ of 9?

wrongAnswers.why: did 9 − 3 — subtracted the denominator
wrongAnswers.remedy: The 3 sets the plates, it doesn't get taken away. Deal 9 into 3 plates.

wrongAnswers.why: confused ⅓ with 'count 1' and answered the plate count
wrongAnswers.remedy: You DO count one plate — but count what's ON it. Three plates, 9 dealt out — how many on each?

reteach.say: Same recipe, new number: ⅓ of 9 means THREE plates. Deal 9: one round — 1 each; two rounds — 2 each; three rounds — 3 each, all gone. One plate holds 3. ⅓ of 9 = 3.

block.prompt: Mystery number! ¼ of my number is 5. What is my whole number?

wrongAnswers.why: added 5 + 4 instead of rebuilding four plates
wrongAnswers.remedy: One plate holds 5 — and there are FOUR plates. Put them all back together.

wrongAnswers.why: divided 5 by 4 or guessed small
wrongAnswers.remedy: The whole is BIGGER than one plate. Four plates of 5 — count them: 5, 10…

hints: One plate = 5. How many plates make the whole?

reteach.say: Run the machine backwards! Normally we share the whole into 4 plates. This time we KNOW one plate — 5 — and rebuild: four plates of 5 is 5, 10, 15, 20. The whole number is 20, because ¼ of 20 = 5. Check it forwards — it works!

block.prompt: A friend says: '¼ of 12 is 8, because 12 − 4 = 8.' What went wrong, and what's the real answer?
block.sample: They took 4 away instead of sharing into 4. ¼ means share 12 into 4 equal piles — 3 in each — so ¼ of 12 = 3.

practiceBank.expectedAnswer: They subtracted instead of sharing; ¼ of 12 = 12 ÷ 4 = 3

wrongAnswers.why: shares the subtract-the-denominator misconception
wrongAnswers.remedy: Test it with sweets: deal 12 onto 4 plates. Does any plate hold 8? What does one plate hold?

wrongAnswers.answer: says it's wrong but can't fix it
wrongAnswers.why: spots the error but the sharing routine isn't secure
wrongAnswers.remedy: Say the recipe together: bottom number 4 → four plates → deal → count one plate.

hints: What does the bottom number really tell you to do?
Deal 12 onto 4 plates and look at one plate.

reteach.say: The 4 in ¼ is not a take-away order — it's a table setting! It says 'set 4 plates'. Deal all 12 fairly: 3 on each plate. One plate — one quarter — is 3. Share, don't subtract: that's the fraction golden rule.

adaptivity.levelUp: 2 consecutive correct at the current level → next level; at level 3, interleave unit fractions, non-unit fractions and the backwards ('¼ of ? = 5') items.
adaptivity.levelDown: 2 misses on the same skill → run that item's reteach with the dealing animated one counter at a time (CPA step down), then serve a level-1 item of the same skill.
adaptivity.masterySignal: 4+ correct across levels 2–3 including one unit fraction, one non-unit fraction (¾), and the routine spoken aloud ('share into 4, count 3') → mastery ≥ 0.8 for 'fractions of a quantity'.
struggleProtocol: Name why: 'the 4 got taken away instead of shared' / 'one plate too few got counted'.
Go fully concrete: deal the counters onto plates together, one at a time.
One hint: 'Bottom number = number of plates.'
Re-ask with ½ of 6, then build back up.
Keep it safe: 'Mistakes show us what to practise — smaller step.'
adaptivity.personalization: Run the fair-share café with the learner's interests — grapes, football cards, gems, dinosaur stickers. The 'say the recipe first' habit (share into __, count __) stays in every framing; never change the numbers.
adaptivity.endOnSuccess: Finish on a winnable share (½ of 6 if needed), then process praise: 'you dealt one-to-each instead of guessing — fair sharing is the secret to fractions.'

differentiation.support: Physically deal into the denominator's number of piles (the KB fix for '12 − 4'); label the plates 1–4; say the recipe aloud before every answer.
differentiation.stretch: Find ⅓ of 9 and ¾ of 8; the backwards puzzle — 'if ¼ of a number is 5, what's the whole number?'

extension: 'Fair feast' — share a bag of (pretend) grapes between the family and write the fraction each person gets; then find ¾ of the bag.
assessmentEvidence: Child finds unit and non-unit fractions of amounts by sharing, links ¼ to ÷ 4, and avoids the subtract-the-denominator error.
revisitLater: Links division (L11) to fractions permanently; quick '¾ of 8?' retrieval in Lesson 25 and the Unit 8 mixed problems.
